threads.thread_goal: Align on current-state process map and main pain points.

messages.text: Sharing a first draft of the current-state map for the intake and handover flow for Integrated Service Lane for Vehicle Sales and Workshop. I based it on what we do today for both sales and service entry points and logged it under T1, with a visual in A1. It covers from first contact at the showroom or phone, through booking, arrival at the lane, and handover to the workshop. Before we lock anything, I would like each of you to check if the steps reflect what really happens on the ground, especially any informal workarounds we rely on.

Thanks for putting A1 together. From the lane side, one thing missing is that we often do a quick visual check in the parking area before the car even reaches the formal intake point. That is where we spot obvious safety issues like fluid leaks or bald tyres. Right now in T1 it looks like the first technical touch is only once the car is in the bay. I suggest we add a step called quick safety walk-around between arrival and paperwork, since it affects how we queue vehicles.

Looking at A1 from the workshop side, I agree with the overall flow. One detail: when sales hands over a vehicle for pre-delivery checks, we usually get the keys and a brief verbal note, but no written description of customer comments. In the map under T1 it shows a standard form, but in practice that is not consistent. Maybe we should mark that as a pain point so we do not assume the form is always there today.

From the sales side, the start of the journey in A1 looks right: greeting, understanding needs, test drive, then either sale or service booking. Where it differs from what I do is the step where we capture technical details. The map shows a structured checklist, but most of us just write free notes in the system or on paper. That is probably why technicians feel they miss information. For T1, should we mark that step as unstructured notes instead of checklist, so we are honest about the current state?

I went through A1 and added comments on the handover and bay assignment parts. Two observations: first, there is no explicit step where the supervisor confirms whether the job is warranty, urgent, or routine before assigning a bay. In reality, we often decide that on the fly, which leads to re-shuffling. Second, the map does not show how we handle overflow when all bays are full; we just park cars wherever we find space. For T1, I suggest we flag both as current gaps rather than trying to design the future state here.

Good catch on the quick safety walk-around. I had not included that as a formal step in A1. For T1 I will add a box between arrival and intake desk called initial safety check in parking area, with technician or lane staff as owner. We should also note that this is not documented today, which might be a root cause for missing safety notes later.

On the inconsistent written description from sales to workshop: I agree we should not show a standard form in the current-state map if it is not actually used. For T1 I will change that step in A1 to say verbal handover plus optional notes, and mark it as a pain point. That will also set us up for the new handover form in T2 later.

Agree on marking the warranty or urgency decision as a separate step. Right now, when that is not clear, we sometimes pull a car out of a bay halfway through to make space for a more urgent job. That is a big source of rework and lost time. For T1, can we highlight that as a bottleneck in A1, maybe with a note that decision criteria are unclear and often made late?

On the missing written description: from my side, the main reason is time at peak hours. If we have a queue of customers, I tend to just write short notes like noise front or service due and rely on the technician to investigate. Maybe in A1 under T1 we should also show that at peak times we skip some questions, so it is clear that the intake is different depending on how busy we are.

That peak-time behaviour is important for the pilot design. For the current-state map in A1, I suggest we add a note on the sales intake step saying that some questions are skipped when there is a queue, leading to incomplete information for the workshop. That will help us later when we look at capacity and rota in T5 and T8.

On overflow handling: from the floor, when bays are full we park cars in the back row and keep keys at the desk. That is not in A1, but it affects how long cars wait before any technician sees them. For T1, maybe we should show a branch after arrival: if bay available, go straight to intake; if not, park in overflow area and wait. That will make the waiting time visible when we later track KPIs in A4.

I have updated A1 with the points raised so far: quick safety walk-around, verbal plus optional notes from sales, explicit urgency or warranty decision, and overflow parking branch. Unless there are strong objections, I propose we treat this as our baseline current-state map for T1 so we can move on to designing improvements. If anyone sees a missing step that would change our pilot decisions, please flag it now.

From my side the updated A1 reflects what we actually do, including the informal steps. I do not see any missing technical actions that would affect the pilot. I am ok to use this as the reference for current intake and handover under T1.

I am also fine with the updated A1 as the baseline. It shows clearly that sales notes are unstructured and that we cut corners when it is busy, which matches my day to day. No further changes from me for T1.

Agreed, A1 now captures the key steps and gaps. To prepare for the pilot, we should also agree on the top pain points we want to tackle first, otherwise we risk spreading efforts too thin. From what I see in T1 and our comments, the main issues are: 1) poor quality of sales-to-workshop handover information, 2) unclear urgency or warranty decision before bay assignment, and 3) peak-time congestion leading to skipped questions and long waits. Do these three sound right as our priorities?

Those three match what I experience. I would only add that safety checks being informal is also a risk, but that might be part of the congestion point. If we can improve the handover and the triage flow, we should be able to formalise the safety walk-around without slowing everything down. I support using your three as the main focus for the pilot.

I agree with those three priorities. From the lane perspective, if we fix the handover quality and the urgency decision, we will already reduce a lot of rework. The congestion piece is where the rota and capacity rules will help later. I am ok to lock these as the top pain points for the pilot design.

Sounds good to me as well. I will update T1 to mark these three as the main pain points linked to A1: handover information, urgency or warranty decision, and peak-time congestion with skipped questions. That will guide the work on T2, T3, and T4. With that, we can consider the current-state map and pain point list closed for this phase.

threads.thread_goal: Define the new intake workflow, handover form, and triage checklist.

messages.text: I have drafted a first version of the sales-to-workshop handover form and script for Integrated Service Lane for Vehicle Sales and Workshop, linked under T2 and stored as A2. The form has sections for customer details, vehicle details, reason for visit, customer observations, and preferred contact method. The script is a short sequence of questions for in-person and phone customers. It is based on the pain points we marked in A1, especially the missing technical details and skipped questions at peak times. I would appreciate feedback on missing fields or anything that feels too long for a busy desk.

I have also uploaded a draft of the service lane intake and triage checklist as A3, linked to T3. It covers three blocks: 1) safety checks at arrival, including leaks, tyres, and warning lights; 2) basic diagnostics, like confirming the symptom, quick road test if needed, and reading fault codes; and 3) documentation, including linking the job to the handover form in A2. The idea is that this checklist can be done within the 20-minute intake target, so I tried to keep it tight. Please check if any steps are unrealistic for the time we have.

Looking at A2, the structure makes sense, but I am concerned about the number of open text fields. For triage and bay allocation in T4, we need at least three items to be standardised: job type (routine, urgent, warranty), expected duration band, and whether the customer is waiting or dropping off. Could we add tick boxes for those, so that we can quickly filter and assign bays according to A5 later?

On A3, the safety block looks good, but the basic diagnostics section might be too heavy for intake. For example, a road test plus fault code read can easily exceed the 20-minute target if we do it for every car. Maybe we should split it: at intake we confirm the symptom and check for obvious issues, and only do road tests or deeper checks if the job is flagged as urgent or safety-related in A2.

I can add tick boxes for job type, expected duration band, and waiting versus drop-off in A2. My only concern is how we estimate duration at the desk. Would it be ok if we use simple bands like up to 1 hour, 1 to 3 hours, and more than 3 hours, based on a quick guideline from you and the technicians? That would keep it manageable for sales staff under T2.

Good point. For A3, I suggest we mark the road test and fault code read as conditional steps. Something like: if symptom is safety-critical or customer is waiting, perform quick road test or code read; otherwise, leave it for the main diagnostic in the bay. That way we respect the 20-minute intake target and still give priority cases more attention.

Those duration bands sound fine. We can prepare a simple cheat sheet for sales with typical times for common jobs, so you are not guessing. For A2 under T2, I would also add a mandatory field for whether parts are likely needed, even if it is just a yes or no based on the symptom. That will help us plan bay usage and parts ordering in T4.

From a customer communication angle, A2 should also capture how and when the customer prefers to be updated. Right now we often call when they expect a message, which leads to complaints. Could we make preferred contact channel and best time to contact mandatory fields? That will also feed into the KPI tracking in A4 later.

Yes, I can make preferred contact channel and best time to contact mandatory in A2. So far the mandatory fields list for the form is: customer and vehicle details, job type, waiting or drop-off, expected duration band, customer observations, safety concerns, likely parts needed yes or no, and contact preferences. If everyone agrees, we can treat that as the core structure for T2.

From the workshop side, that list of mandatory fields in A2 would give us enough to start work without chasing extra information. The key for us is having clear job type, symptom description, and whether the customer is waiting. I support locking this structure so we can move on to training in T6 later.

Agreed. With those mandatory fields in A2, we can link the form directly into the triage checklist in A3. For example, the job type and waiting or drop-off fields can drive which triage path we follow. I am ok to consider the form structure approved for T2.

On A3, I like the three-block structure. To make it workable in the lane, I suggest we define a target time for each block: safety checks within 5 minutes, symptom confirmation within 10 minutes, and documentation within 5 minutes. That keeps us within the 20-minute intake target. We should also specify that only the safety and symptom confirmation are mandatory for every job; the conditional deeper checks apply only to urgent or safety-critical cases as you and 20895 suggested.

I can update A3 to reflect those time targets and mark which steps are mandatory versus conditional. That will also help when we brief technicians under T7. Once that is done, the checklist will have a clear sequence: safety, symptom confirmation, then documentation, with optional deeper checks based on job type and waiting status from A2.

Please also make sure A3 includes a step to confirm that all mandatory fields from A2 are filled before we move the car to a bay. That will reduce back-and-forth between sales and technicians. Once that is in, I think we can treat the triage checklist steps and timing as agreed for T3.

I have added that cross-check step between A2 and A3. With the time targets and conditional checks defined, I am comfortable saying the triage checklist is ready from a technical side. It fits within the 20-minute intake window and supports bay allocation rules in A5.

With the latest updates, we now have: a handover form in A2 with a clear set of mandatory fields, and a triage checklist in A3 with defined steps and timing. From a coordination point of view, I consider both approved for use in the pilot, and we can now finalise the lane workflow and bay allocation rules in T4.

threads.thread_goal: Lock in lane capacity rules, staff rota, and pilot schedule.

messages.text: I have put together a draft staff rota and lane capacity rules for the pilot of Integrated Service Lane for Vehicle Sales and Workshop. The rota is in A8, linked to T5, and the bay allocation rules are in A5, linked to T4. The proposal is a two-week pilot, Monday to Friday, with one dedicated seller at the lane during peak hours, two technicians rotating on intake, and the supervisor overseeing bay allocation. Please review if the shifts and rules are realistic with our current headcount.

Thanks for sharing A8 and A5. On the capacity rules, I see we are assuming a maximum of four simultaneous intake cases per hour, based on the 20-minute target and two technicians. Given the conditional checks in A3, that seems reasonable, but we should also define what happens when more than four cars arrive in the same hour. A5 mentions overflow to standard bays, but we might need a simple rule like: if queue exceeds three cars, convert some to drop-off with later triage.

Looking at A8, the rotation of technicians on intake versus bay work is ok for weekdays, but on Saturdays we usually have fewer people. I do not see Saturday in the pilot schedule. Are we planning to exclude Saturdays from the pilot, or should we add a lighter version of the rota for that day? It will affect how we interpret KPIs in A4 later.

On the seller side, A8 shows one dedicated seller at the lane from 9 to 12 and 14 to 17. That leaves early morning and late afternoon without a dedicated person. In practice, we get a few walk-ins around 8:30 and close to 18:00. Should we define in A5 that outside peak hours, the showroom seller on duty covers the lane, using the same A2 form, so we do not create a gap in the process?

Good point on Saturdays. To keep the pilot manageable with current staff, I suggest we limit the formal integrated lane pilot to weekdays only for the first two weeks. Saturdays would continue with the existing process, and we would not include those days in the KPI tracker A4. I will note that in T5 and T8 so we are clear on scope.

I am ok with limiting the pilot to weekdays for now, as long as we clearly mark that in A4 and in the final report under T12. For the overflow rule you mentioned earlier, I propose we add to A5: if more than three cars are waiting for intake, the supervisor can switch some to drop-off mode, with triage scheduled later in the day, and communicate expected timing using the contact preferences from A2.

That overflow rule works for the lane team. If we can convert some arrivals to drop-off when the queue is long, we will avoid rushed intakes that skip safety checks. We just need to make sure the rota in A8 has at least one technician available later in the day to handle those delayed triage cases, not only bay work.

I am fine with covering the lane outside peak hours as the showroom seller on duty, as long as we keep the A2 form simple enough to handle both showroom and lane customers. Maybe in A8 we can just note that outside 9 to 12 and 14 to 17, the on-duty seller is responsible for intake, and we do not promise the 20-minute target during those times.

Summarising the pilot schedule proposal: two-week pilot, weekdays only, with the integrated lane running from 8:30 to 18:00, but with dedicated lane staff only from 9 to 12 and 14 to 17 as per A8. Outside those peak windows, the on-duty showroom seller and one technician will handle intake using the same A2 and A3, but we will track intake times separately in A4. If there are no objections, I would like to confirm this as our pilot start and duration.

From the workshop side, that schedule is workable. A two-week weekday pilot gives us enough volume to see patterns without overloading the team. I support confirming that as the pilot start and duration, assuming we can brief everyone the day before as part of T7 and T6.

Agreed on the two-week weekday pilot with the described hours. I will plan the issue log and daily summaries under T9 around that window. Let us lock that in so we can finalise the rota and bay rules.

I have updated A8 so that one of the technicians on the late shift is explicitly assigned to handle delayed triage cases from the overflow rule in A5, not just bay work. I also added notes about weekday-only pilot and peak versus off-peak coverage. Unless anyone sees a gap, I suggest we treat the rota and bay allocation rules as final for the pilot.
The updated A8 and A5 look good to me. The intake rotation, overflow handling, and late-shift triage are all clear. From the lane team perspective, we can work with this setup for the pilot.

I am also fine with the rota and bay rules as described in A8 and A5. The coverage for sales is clear, and the overflow rule gives us a way to manage queues without rushing. I consider the rota and allocation rules agreed for the pilot.

With the pilot dates, rota in A8, and bay rules in A5 all aligned, we are ready to move into pre-pilot readiness checks and training. I will coordinate with you on T7 and with sales on T6 so that everyone understands their slots and the overflow rules before day one.

threads.thread_goal: Monitor pilot progress, surface issues, and adjust quickly.

messages.text: First day of the integrated lane pilot for Integrated Service Lane for Vehicle Sales and Workshop is done. I have entered the initial KPIs into A4 under T9 and T8. Headline numbers: average intake time was 23 minutes versus our 20-minute target, with 60 percent of cases within target. We had three incidents logged in the daily issue log for T9: one missed safety check from A3, one incomplete A2 form causing a delay, and one case where overflow rules in A5 were not applied and the queue reached five cars. Let us use this thread to capture observations and decide if we need any immediate tweaks.

From the lane side, the main reason for intake times going over 20 minutes was that we tried to do road tests for almost every noise complaint, even though A3 says those are conditional. That added 5 to 10 minutes per case. Also, the missed safety check incident happened when we were rushing to catch up with the queue. We might need to reinforce that safety block is non-negotiable, even if we have to delay some non-urgent diagnostics.

I handled two of the cases where the A2 form was incomplete. In both, the job type and waiting or drop-off fields were missing, so we had to call the seller back. That added about 10 minutes. Maybe we should add a quick check at the intake desk to confirm that all mandatory fields in A2 are filled before the customer leaves, not only when the car reaches the technician.

From the sales side, the new A2 form worked, but during the morning peak I struggled to keep up with the script and fill all fields. I noticed I was spending extra time on open text for customer observations. Maybe we can add a few common options to tick, like noise, vibration, warning light, service due, and then use a shorter text box for details. That might speed up completion and reduce missing fields.

I was on the floor during the afternoon peak when the queue reached five cars. The overflow rule in A5 was not applied because the supervisor on duty was busy resolving a warranty dispute. The team hesitated to convert arrivals to drop-off without explicit approval. We might need to clarify in A5 that the intake technician can trigger the overflow rule when the queue exceeds three cars, and then inform the supervisor, instead of waiting for a decision.

Agree that we should not be doing road tests for every noise complaint at intake. A3 clearly marks those as conditional. For the rest of this week, I propose we tighten the rule: only do a road test at intake if the symptom is safety-critical or if the customer is waiting and the job type is urgent. All other cases should go straight to bay diagnostics after the basic checks. That should help bring average intake time closer to 20 minutes.

I can brief the lane technicians on that tighter rule before the next shift. We will stick to basic checks and symptom confirmation for most cases, and reserve road tests for safety-critical or urgent waiting jobs as defined in A2. I will also remind everyone that the safety block in A3 must be completed for every car, even if the queue is long.

On the incomplete A2 forms, I can add a quick self-check step to my routine: before handing the form over, I will scan for job type, waiting or drop-off, and contact details. If we agree on a short checklist for sellers, I can also share it with the rest of the team as part of T6 so we all follow the same habit.

Adding common options to tick for customer observations in A2 would help. From the workshop side, having standard categories like noise, vibration, warning light, and performance issue would also make it easier to scan the forms quickly. As long as there is still a small text box for extra detail, that change should not affect our diagnostics.

On the overflow rule, I support giving intake technicians the authority to trigger it when the queue exceeds three cars, as long as they log it in the T9 issue log and inform the supervisor as soon as possible. We can update A5 to reflect that and mention it in the next daily briefing.

I will update A5 with that change and make sure it is highlighted in tomorrow morning's check-in. That should prevent queues from growing unchecked when the supervisor is tied up. We will also watch the impact on intake times in A4 over the next few days.

To summarise the proposed tweaks after day one: 1) enforce safety checks in A3 as mandatory for every car; 2) restrict road tests at intake to safety-critical or urgent waiting jobs; 3) add tick-box categories for customer observations in A2 and a quick self-check for sellers; and 4) allow intake technicians to trigger the overflow rule in A5 when the queue exceeds three cars, logging it in T9. If everyone agrees, we will apply these changes from tomorrow and monitor the effect in A4 for the rest of the first week.

That summary matches what we discussed. From the lane team, we can implement all four points immediately. I expect the stricter rule on road tests and the clearer overflow authority to have the biggest impact on intake times and queue length.

I am aligned with those tweaks as well. I will adjust A2 with the tick-box options and share a short reminder with the sales team about the self-check on mandatory fields. We will start using the updated form from tomorrow morning.

From the workshop side, I support all four changes. They should reduce rework and help us stay closer to the 20-minute intake target without compromising safety. I will keep an eye on how many cases still exceed the target in A4 and flag anything unusual in the T9 log.

Great, we will treat these four items as our agreed immediate adjustments after the first pilot days. I will update A3, A2, and A5 accordingly and continue to track the impact in A4 for the weekly review.

threads.thread_goal: Review pilot results, customer feedback, and next steps.

messages.text: I have uploaded a draft pilot report for Integrated Service Lane for Vehicle Sales and Workshop under T12, using data from A4 and customer feedback from A7. Headline results: average intake time over the two-week pilot was 19 minutes, down from 23 on day one; rework cases due to poor handover dropped by 40 percent; and customer satisfaction on intake improved, with 85 percent of respondents in A7 rating the experience as good or very good. There are still some issues around peak-time congestion and occasional missed documentation steps. We need to decide whether to make the integrated lane process permanent and what improvements to prioritise next.

Looking at A4 and A7, the main strengths of the new process are clear: more consistent handovers thanks to A2, better safety coverage with A3, and clearer expectations set with customers. The remaining pain points seem to be: 1) occasional queues above three cars when multiple walk-ins arrive at once, and 2) some variation in how strictly the overflow rule in A5 is applied. From an operations perspective, I would recommend we keep the integrated lane and focus on fine-tuning capacity and training rather than going back to the old process.

From the lane team, the new workflow is a big improvement. The triage checklist in A3 helped us catch several safety issues early, and the clearer handover from A2 reduced the number of times we had to call sales back. The main stress points were on Monday mornings and late Fridays, where even with the overflow rule in A5 we felt stretched. If we keep the lane permanently, I would suggest we look at adding a floating technician during those peak windows, even if it means adjusting other tasks.

I agree that the new process is better overall. One thing I noticed in A4 is that the few rework cases we still had were mostly linked to incomplete or unclear customer observations in A2, especially for intermittent issues. Maybe we should add a short prompt in the script to ask when the issue happens and how often, so we get more precise information without adding much time.

Customer feedback in A7 was mostly positive about the clearer explanations and estimated times. A few comments mentioned that the form felt long, especially when there was a queue. If we keep the lane, I would like to simplify the script slightly, maybe by combining some questions or using more tick boxes, while keeping the mandatory fields that technicians rely on.

Given the improvements in A4 and the positive feedback in A7, I am inclined to propose that we adopt the integrated lane as our standard process, with some adjustments. Before we confirm that, are there any strong reasons from your sides to stop the lane or go back to the previous way of working?

No strong reasons to stop from me. The new process is more structured and safer. The only condition I would add is that we keep monitoring intake times and safety compliance using A4 and A6, and that we schedule regular refreshers for technicians so the checklist in A3 does not become a formality.

From sales, I would also support keeping the integrated lane. It gives customers a clearer path and reduces confusion about who they should talk to. I just want to make sure we keep refining A2 so it stays practical during busy times, and that we plan short refresh sessions under T6 when we update the script.

I am aligned with making the lane permanent. To address the remaining congestion issues, I suggest three improvement actions for the next quarter: 1) adjust the rota in A8 to add a floating technician during the known peak windows, 2) refine the overflow rules in A5 with clearer triggers and communication steps, and 3) run a joint refresher session for sales and technicians on A2 and A3, using examples from the T9 issue log.

Those three actions make sense. I would add that we should use A6 to run a quick safety and warranty compliance review of the final process, just to be sure that none of the shortcuts we introduced during the pilot conflict with requirements. Once that is done, I would be comfortable with the lane as our standard way of working.

Based on your feedback and the data in A4 and A7, I propose the following: we roll out the integrated lane process permanently, keep monitoring KPIs in A4, and implement the improvement actions you listed: rota adjustment in A8, refined overflow rules in A5, joint refresher training on A2 and A3, and a safety and warranty review using A6. If there are no objections, I will update T12 to reflect this decision and action plan.

I support that proposal. Making the lane permanent with those follow-up actions will help us keep the gains from the pilot and continue improving. I am happy to help with the safety and compliance review using A6 and to share examples from the lane for the refresher sessions.
I am aligned as well. I will take the lead on updating the A2 script based on A7 feedback and plan a short refresher for the sales team, so the permanent process starts on the right foot.

Count me in. I will adjust the rota in A8, refine A5 with the updated overflow rules, and coordinate the joint refresher session using cases from T9. We can then close out T12 with the final report and agreed action owners.

Great, I will update T12 to state that we are rolling out the integrated lane process permanently, with the improvement actions and owners we just agreed. I will also schedule a follow-up review in one month to look at updated KPIs in A4 and any new feedback in A7.
